rows.description: My mother finds a note and laughs or gets angry, and I feel exposed. A good parent stays calm, says it is natural, and talks about respect and boundaries. I can ask that they keep it private.
My friends chant our names together and I feel humiliated. I can say stop, that is not fun for me. Real friends stop when asked. Teasing about a crush can hurt both children and spoil a friendship.

I found out my crush likes someone else and my chest feels heavy. This ache is real, though it will pass. Wise: cry if needed, talk to someone, stay friends if I can. Mocking him or the other kid does not help.
Classmates tease me that a boy likes me, and I go red. His feelings are his own and I do not have to feel the same. I can say thanks for being nice, but I am not thinking about that, and stay kind.
A classmate laughs at my marks. It hurts, but I know one score does not define me. I can answer calmly or walk away, and remember that he too has weak spots.
My parent shouts about my failure and I go quiet. I feel small. I can wait until things cool, then say I want to improve and ask for help with a plan.
My friend says he also struggled and offers to study together. I feel less alone. Shared effort turns a failure into a team problem with a solution.
I failed and I feel like the whole class knows I am stupid. Shame makes me hide, but a failed test is information about what to practise, not a label on me.
A tired parent who comes home glued to the phone gives the child no eye contact, so the child escalates with whining or mess to be noticed. A few minutes of warm, undivided attention prevents this.
The toddler runs, clings, smiles or bursts into tears at reunion: relief that the safe person is back. Caregiver should kneel, hold and say I am here, giving time before the next activity.
After a long day away the child follows father everywhere and wails if he steps out of sight. It is normal need to refill security, not spoiling. Give short, full-attention time before chores.
Shadows and sounds feel big to a mind that cannot yet tell real from imagined. Respond with a night light, calm voice and closeness; never mock, and never use ghosts or bogeymen as threat.
The child cries when the parent leaves, wanting touch and voice to fall asleep. Consistent short routines, a lullaby and a gentle goodnight help her learn safety without abrupt abandonment.
Being shut in alone and ignored while crying overwhelms a very young child; she may stop crying not from calm but from giving up. Respond warmly, staying present as sleep habits build.
A teacher stays after class to explain what I missed. I feel thankful and a little embarrassed to need help. Wise: say thanks and use the time well; asking is strength.
I am being measured by marks, and it feels like love is conditional. Wise: hear the fear behind their push and say what helps, like a plan or a calm evening. Harmful: shutting down.
My friend has stopped eating and sleeping before boards. Wise: sit with them, offer a break, and tell a parent or counsellor if they sound hopeless. Harmful: joking or ignoring it.
A coaching centre ranks students in batches and makes the low-ranked feel lesser to sell fear. Wise: notice the business model, keep my own pace, and talk to a trusted adult if I am crumbling.

My sick brother gets all the attention and I feel jealous, then guilty. Both feelings are normal. I can ask for a little time with my parents and still care for my brother. Feeling this does not make me bad.
My mother is unwell and I worry about her all day at school. Worry shows love. Wise: ask what I can help with, keep my routine and tell my teacher. I am not responsible for curing her.
My younger sister is in the hospital and I draw pictures for her. Small acts connect us. I am allowed to be sad and also to play. Feeling guilty when I am happy helps nobody.
